title: Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis

paper.title: Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but an
advantage-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting
target distribution. We propose
Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement
learning (RL) method for Kullback–Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement
through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the
advantage function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy.
A Doob h h -transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference
diffusion drift. We derive a posterior-mean representation of the correction
and estimate it using paired self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS).
Supervised regression on these drift targets updates the neural actor
without critic action gradients. In the small-update regime, the
KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the
Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts.
Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the
effects of critic estimation, neural drift regression, finite-sample SNIS,
diffusion discretization, and inherited actor error on expected average policy
suboptimality. Synthetic experiments assess the accuracy of approximation to prescribed
advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to sampling budgets. On six
offline-to-online continuous-control tasks, a reference-anchored implementation
achieves higher final-window returns than those of its corresponding offline
initialization.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Offline RL learns a policy from previously collected transitions without further interaction with the environment. The accuracy of its value estimates depends on the state–action coverage of these data ( Levine et al., 2020 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ; Kostrikov et al., 2022 ) . Offline-to-online (O2O) RL combines offline data or pretrained policies with subsequent online learning ( Nair et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Ball et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . This transition requires adapting to new experience while retaining useful information from the offline data. In the early online stages, value estimates remain influenced by offline coverage: favoring poorly covered actions can amplify estimation error, whereas restrictive policy updates can limit adaptation. Policy representation introduces a further challenge: offline datasets may combine several behavior policies and contain multiple plausible actions at the same state. Diffusion actors accommodate the resulting multimodal conditional action distributions ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . They define policies through a generative process without requiring an explicit conditional density. Policy improvement therefore requires modifying this process to sample from the action distribution prescribed by estimated value information. To formulate this problem, we follow advantage-weighted and product-policy approaches to policy improvement ( Peng et al., 2019 ; Nair et al., 2020 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) and use A π ​ ( s , a ) A^{\pi}(s,a) to measure the quality of an action relative to the current policy. For a reference policy π \pi and regularization parameter λ > 0 \lambda>0 , the improved policy at state s s is defined by π ¯ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ∈ argmax π ′ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) { 𝔼 a ∼ π ′ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) [ A π ( s , a ) ] − λ KL ( π ′ ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ∥ π ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ) } , \bar{\pi}(\cdot\mid s)\in\argmax_{\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s)}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s)}[A^{\pi}(s,a)]-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s)\,\middle\|\,\pi(\cdot\mid s)\right)\right\}, whose solution is the exponential tilt π ¯ ​ ( a ∣ s ) = π ⁡ ( a ∣ s ) ​ exp ⁡ A π ​ ( s , a ) / λ ∫ 𝒜 π ⁡ ( a ′ ∣ s ) ​ exp ⁡ A π ​ ( s , a ′ ) / λ , d ​ a ′ . \bar{\pi}(a\mid s)=\frac{\pi(a\mid s)\exp{A^{\pi}(s,a)/\lambda}}{\int_{\mathcal{A}}\pi(a^{\prime}\mid s)\exp{A^{\pi}(s,a^{\prime})/\lambda},\mathrm{d}a^{\prime}}. (1) For an implicit diffusion actor, ( 1 ) specifies the target distribution but does not provide the diffusion dynamics needed to generate it. Realizing this KL-regularized update therefore requires a corresponding change in the diffusion drift. Existing generative-policy methods incorporate value information through critic action gradients, actor-parameter optimization, or reweighting of sampled candidate actions ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2023a ; Park et al., 2025 ) . A complementary approach is to estimate the drift implied by the prescribed tilt from policy samples and pointwise advantage evaluations. Such a construction would permit supervised actor fitting without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. Its statistical accuracy, however, depends on both the estimated advantage and the approximation of the target diffusion. Errors from critic estimation, drift learning, and numerical sampling can propagate through successive policy updates. An exact tilting identity alone does not control these effects. This motivates a joint construction and analysis that connects the prescribed target, the learned diffusion drift, and the resulting policy performance. To address these issues, we propose Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online method for KL-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. SFAC represents the current policy as the terminal law of a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer diffusion ( Föllmer, 1985 ; Föllmer, 1986 ; Föllmer, 1988 ) . Reweighting this terminal law induces a change of measure on path space, which a Doob h h -transform realizes through a drift correction ( Doob, 1984 ; Baudoin, 2002 ) . Here h h is the positive conditional expectation, under the reference diffusion, of the terminal reweighting factor given the current diffusion state. Applying this construction to the advantage tilt gives a target diffusion whose terminal law is the prescribed policy update. The learned actor and its numerical sampler approximate this exact representation. Specifically, at iteration k k , let π k \pi_{k} denote the current practical policy and A ^ k \widehat{A}_{k} the minimax Bellman critic’s estimate of its advantage A π k A^{\pi_{k}} . The resulting plug-in target π ¯ k + 1 \bar{\pi}_{k+1} satisfies π ¯ k + 1 ​ ( a ∣ s ) ∝ π k ​ ( a ∣ s ) ​ exp ⁡ { A ^ k ​ ( s , a ) / λ } \bar{\pi}_{k+1}(a\mid s)\propto\pi_{k}(a\mid s)\exp\{\widehat{A}_{k}(s,a)/\lambda\} . Here ∝ \propto denotes equality up to a state-dependent normalizing factor. The drift correction is a time-scaled difference between the posterior means under the advantage-tilted and reference distributions. Paired self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) estimates these means from shared terminal-action samples. Adding the resulting Monte Carlo correction to the current learned drift produces regression targets for the updated neural actor. Euler–Maruyama simulation of this actor defines the practical policy π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} , which approximates π ¯ k + 1 \bar{\pi}_{k+1} . The actor update therefore uses supervised drift regression without critic action gradients. In the small-update regime, the ideal exponential tilt follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same first-order change in the space of diffusion drifts. We then analyze how the approximation errors affect policy performance. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds for advantage estimation under dependent transition data, actor regression, SNIS, and time discretization. Combining these bounds with the inherited actor error yields a bound on expected average policy suboptimality across iterations. The analysis separates the contributions of the statistical and computational budgets; it does not cover neural-network optimization or replay-buffer management. We complement this analysis with experiments on the sampling construction and its use in online policy refinement. Controlled examples use two- and four-component Gaussian mixtures to assess approximation to specified advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to the endpoint sample size m m and diffusion-step count T T . We also evaluate a reference-anchored implementation on six continuous-control tasks from Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning (D4RL) ( Fu et al., 2020 ) . Under the reported protocol for interaction, replay, and evaluation, its final-window normalized return exceeds that of the corresponding offline initialization on all six tasks.

sections.heading: 1.1 Contributions
sections.text: Our contributions are as follows. • A conditional-diffusion formulation of policy improvement. We formulate KL-regularized policy improvement for diffusion actors through a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer process. The exponential advantage tilt defines a terminal change of measure, and the corresponding Doob h h -transform identifies the drift correction that realizes the improved policy. In the small-update regime, the ideal KL step follows the natural policy-gradient direction, while the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. • Sample-based actor learning without critic action gradients. The Doob correction is the difference between advantage-tilted and reference posterior means. We estimate this difference by paired self-normalized importance sampling using current-policy samples and pointwise advantage evaluations, then fit the next drift network by supervised regression. This update does not require critic action gradients. • Finite-sample guarantees. We bound actor estimation error in Wasserstein distance and reverse KL divergence, separating the contributions of neural drift regression, finite-sample SNIS, Euler–Maruyama discretization, and inherited reference-drift error. Combining this result with critic estimation under dependent transition data yields a bound on expected average policy suboptimality across policy iterations. • Empirical evidence. We evaluate our method for offline-to-online policy improvement. Synthetic experiments evaluate approximation to prescribed advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to the endpoint-sample and diffusion-step budgets. On six D4RL continuous-control tasks, the reference-anchored implementation improves its final-window performance relative to the corresponding offline initialization.

sections.heading: Offline and offline-to-online RL.
sections.text: Offline RL addresses distribution shift through conservative action-value estimation, behavior-regularized policy learning, or implicit policy extraction ( Kumar et al., 2020 ; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Kostrikov et al., 2022 ) . The transition to online learning also requires preserving useful offline behavior while adapting to new experience. Advantage-weighted actor–critic (AWAC) uses weighted maximum-likelihood actor updates, calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL) controls the scale of conservative action-value estimates, and policy expansion (PEX) combines a frozen offline policy with a learnable policy ( Nair et al., 2020 ; Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . RL with prior data (RLPD) instead incorporates offline transitions directly into online off-policy training, without requiring offline pretraining ( Ball et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion models can also augment the training distribution: synthetic experience replay (SynthER) generates additional replay data, whereas energy-guided diffusion sampling (EDIS) guides synthetic transitions toward the current online distribution ( Lu et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . These methods generate transitions; SFAC instead updates conditional action distributions. Fitted policy iteration and minimax Bellman methods relate estimation error to policy performance under approximation and coverage conditions ( Antos et al., 2008 ; Xie and Jiang, 2020b ) . Deep approximate policy iteration further combines neural approximation, Bellman-residual estimation under dependent data, and error propagation ( Jiao et al., 2025 ) . Minimax off-policy evaluation separately studies the statistical estimation of policy returns ( Uehara et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2021 ) , while policy-finetuning theory quantifies the role of reference-policy coverage in sample-efficient online adaptation ( Xie et al., 2021b ) . SFAC addresses the additional actor-learning and numerical-sampling errors introduced by conditional diffusion policy updates.

sections.heading: Generative policies.
sections.text: Denoising and score-based diffusion models provide flexible distributional representations ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Diffuser and Decision Diffuser generate trajectories for planning, whereas Diffusion Policy generates observation-conditioned action sequences ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) . For action-level policy improvement, Diffusion-QL combines denoising regression with action-value maximization ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Implicit diffusion Q-learning (IDQL) reweights candidates from a diffusion behavior model and also considers online fine-tuning ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Contrastive energy prediction (CEP) learns intermediate energy guidance for Q-guided policy optimization (QGPO), with population consistency under unlimited model capacity and data ( Lu et al., 2023a ) . Diffusion actor–critic (DAC) expresses behavior-constrained policy improvement as noise regression with a critic-action-gradient correction ( Fang et al., 2025 ) . Classifier-free guidance for RL (CFGRL) instead trains an optimality-conditioned generative model and adjusts its guidance strength at sampling time ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Flow Q-Learning trains a one-step actor using a flow behavior model and includes O2O evaluation ( Park et al., 2025 ) ; diffusion policy policy optimization (DPPO) fine-tunes diffusion policies by applying policy optimization to coupled denoising and environment dynamics ( Ren et al., 2025 ) . These methods differ in how action-value information enters the policy update. SFAC uses paired SNIS to estimate posterior-mean drift corrections and refits a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer actor by supervised regression. Its distinguishing feature is this drift-target construction, rather than KL regularization or actor refitting alone.

sections.heading: Regularized updates and controlled diffusion.
sections.text:
Relative-entropy policy search and KL-constrained policy optimization motivate exponential reweighting relative to a reference distribution ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2019 ) . Maximum-entropy RL promotes policy entropy, while regularized Bellman theory provides a broader framework for penalty-based updates and their error propagation ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ; Geist et al., 2019 ) . On path space, Föllmer’s entropy construction and the Doob h h -transform connect terminal reweighting to a change in diffusion drift ( Föllmer, 1985 ; Föllmer, 1986 ; Föllmer, 1988 ; Doob, 1984 ) . Schrödinger–Föllmer samplers realize a target law at a finite terminal time, without an ergodic limit; their nonasymptotic analyses allow non-log-concave targets under suitable regularity conditions ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Jiao et al., 2026 ) . Diffusion Schrödinger bridges address the related problem of entropy-regularized transport between endpoint distributions ( De Bortoli et al., 2021 ) . For pretrained diffusion models, entropy-regularized control yields reward-based fine-tuning objectives ( Uehara et al., 2024a ) , and feedback-efficient methods combine reward learning, exploration, and generative updates with regret guarantees ( Uehara et al., 2024b ) . Recent theory establishes regularity preservation and convergence of control-policy iteration ( Han et al., 2025 ) , regression-based statistical guarantees for diffusion fine-tuning ( Mou, 2025 ) , and nonasymptotic guidance and distributional bounds for learned Doob h h -transforms ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . Finite-particle approximations can nevertheless bias the intended tilt, even in tractable Gaussian examples ( Dandapanthula and Boffi, 2026 ) . An exact change-of-measure identity therefore does not establish the accuracy of an estimated and discretized actor. SFAC complements these results by propagating Bellman-critic, posterior-mean, drift-regression, and discretization errors through successive policy updates. The resulting guarantee concerns expected average suboptimality under regularity, coverage, and stability conditions, not improvement of every fitted policy. sections.heading: 1.3 Outline
sections.text: Section 2 introduces the notation and reviews the relevant RL and Schrödinger–Föllmer preliminaries. Section 3 develops advantage estimation with a minimax Bellman critic and conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer policy improvement. Section 4 analyzes advantage estimation, actor approximation, and their propagation through policy iteration. Section 5 outlines the main proofs, and Section 6 presents the numerical experiments. Section 7 concludes. Complete proofs and auxiliary results appear in the appendix.

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: This section introduces the notation, RL framework, and function classes and reviews the Schrödinger–Föllmer representation underlying the diffusion actor.

sections.heading: 4 Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: This section analyzes advantage estimation and conditional diffusion sampling and then relates their errors to policy performance. Section 4.1 bounds the mean-square advantage-estimation error under dependent observations. Section 4.2 bounds the actor’s squared Wasserstein and reverse-KL errors relative to the plug-in target, with KL measured from the target to the practical policy. Section 4.3 combines these results to bound the expected average policy suboptimality.

Assumption 4.1 imposes uniform concentrability: the sampling law covers every admissible state–action distribution with a bounded density ratio. A similar condition appears in Assumption 1 of Chen and Jiang (2019) ; related concentrability coefficients are used by Antos et al. (2008) and Xie and Jiang (2020b) . Assumption 4.2 controls the tails of the current and one-step state–action laws, making errors outside expanding compact sets negligible even on unbounded domains. Bounded-design approximation is used in Section 4.2 of Feng et al. (2023) , while Section 2.1 of Jiao et al. (2025) assumes bounded state and action spaces. On a common bounded state–action domain, both exponential-moment bounds hold automatically. The explicit tail condition here extends the analysis to unbounded support; it differs from the bounded-domain conditions in those papers. Assumption 4.3 requires Hölder regularity of Bellman images so that the auxiliary neural network class can approximate them. It is a smoothness-based counterpart of the Bellman-completeness condition in Assumption 3 of Chen and Jiang (2019) . Hölder regularity of Bellman targets is used in Theorem 21 and Remark 22 of Feng et al. (2023) and in the deep policy-iteration analysis of Jiao et al. (2025) . The condition does not require exact closure of a finite network class under the Bellman operator; approximation error is controlled through network size. The separate smoothness condition on Q π k Q^{\pi_{k}} is needed to approximate the action-value function itself; smoothness of A π k A^{\pi_{k}} alone does not imply this condition. Theorem 4.1 establishes mean-square consistency of A ^ k \widehat{A}_{k} , uniformly over iterations and admissible distributions. Its rate balances neural approximation and statistical error under dependent observations. Blocking yields the effective sample size ξ n ≍ n / ( log ⁡ n ) 1 / η \xi_{n}\asymp n/(\log n)^{1/\eta} , so exponential mixing affects the stated polynomial rate only through logarithmic factors. (16) Remark 4.2 . Assumption 4.4 imposes joint smoothness and uniform positivity on the reference and target density ratios relative to the Gaussian measure. This condition complements the two local representations in Section A . Proposition A.1 describes the ideal update in a smooth parametric policy family, where regularity of log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) \log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) and nondegeneracy of the Fisher matrix yield a well-defined natural policy-gradient expansion. Proposition A.2 represents the same local update through the Doob correction of the SF drift. Accordingly, Assumption 4.4 provides the regularity needed for this diffusion representation: positivity prevents degeneracy of the logarithmic derivatives defining the drift, while smoothness controls the density-to-drift map and supports neural approximation and time discretization. Related density-ratio conditions are standard in nonasymptotic SF analyses ( Jiao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) ; here they are imposed jointly in the state and action variables, with additional smoothness to control time derivatives of the heat semigroup. From an actor–critic viewpoint ( Wu et al., 2020 ; Chen and Zhao, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , this is analogous to assuming bounded or Lipschitz policy scores for a parametric actor: both ensure that a local policy update induces a controlled change in its representation. The difference is that classical actor–critic theory regularizes the map θ ↦ π θ \theta\mapsto\pi_{\theta} , whereas SFAC regularizes the induced density-to-drift map. This is an additional condition on the plug-in target and is not implied by the ReLU critic specification. Assumption 4.5 controls higher moments of the normalized importance weights over the actor design and time grid. Its connection to Section A is through the same exponential change of measure. Proposition A.1 shows that, to first order in λ − 1 \lambda^{-1} , the ideal exponential tilt gives an advantage-weighted natural policy-gradient update, whereas Proposition A.2 realizes this update through the Doob correction. The normalized bridge weights in SFAC therefore play the role of policy likelihood ratios in a parametric actor. Standard actor–critic, trust-region, and off-policy analyses control such ratios through KL bounds or moment conditions on policy-density ratios ( Wu et al., 2020 ; Chen and Zhao, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) ; SFAC imposes the corresponding condition on the normalized weights generated by exp ⁡ { A ^ k / λ } \exp\{\widehat{A}_{k}/\lambda\} . Importance-sampling theory likewise relates estimator accuracy to target–proposal overlap and density-ratio moments ( Agapiou et al., 2017 ; Chatterjee and Diaconis, 2018 ) . The ( 4 + δ ρ ) (4+\delta_{\rho}) -moment requirement is stronger than the usual second-moment condition because paired SNIS involves both a random denominator and increasing endpoint sensitivity of the posterior-mean response; the time averaging accounts for this effect explicitly. Thus, Assumption 4.5 is the SF analogue of likelihood-ratio or trust-region stability. The same parameter λ \lambda links the two views: λ − 1 \lambda^{-1} is the local natural policy-gradient step size, while in SFAC it also controls the concentration of the exponential weights and hence the stability of SNIS. Assumption 4.6 controls the within-round distribution shift between the bridge-training design and the learned Euler path. This condition plays the same role as concentrability conditions used to transfer estimation errors across distributions in batch RL ( Chen and Jiang, 2019 ; Xie and Jiang, 2020b ; Xie et al., 2021b ) . Theorem 4.2 controls expected squared Wasserstein error and reverse KL divergence from the plug-in target to the practical policy, averaged over d π ⋆ d^{\pi^{\star}} . The four contributions are neural regression and approximation, Euler discretization, finite- m m SNIS estimation, and inherited reference-drift error. Consequently, increasing the training sample size alone is insufficient for convergence: m m and T T must be chosen jointly, and the inherited error must also vanish. The proof combines Lemma 5.10 with coupling and change-of-measure arguments.

Then 𝔼 ⁡ [ 1 K ​ ∑ k = 0 K − 1 ( J ⁡ ( π ⋆ ) − J ⁡ ( π k ) ) ] ≲ 1 ( 1 − γ ) 2 ​ 𝒪 ~ ​ ( n − ζ 2 ​ d + 4 ​ ζ ) . \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\bigl(J(\pi^{\star})-J(\pi_{k})\bigr)\right]\lesssim\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{-\frac{\zeta}{2d+4\zeta}}\right). Remark 4.3 . Assumption 4.7 provides the change-of-measure conditions used in the policy-performance analysis. Its state-occupancy bounds relate the current, plug-in target, and comparator distributions, allowing critic and policy-approximation errors to be evaluated under a common reference distribution, as in concentrability-based RL analyses ( Chen and Jiang, 2019 ; Xie and Jiang, 2020b ; Xie et al., 2021a ; Zhan et al., 2022 ) . The action-level bound complements this state coverage by requiring the plug-in target to dominate the comparator policy at each state; state-occupancy coverage alone does not imply this action-level domination, and the assumption does not assert monotonic policy improvement. The general bound ( 17 ) retains the average inherited drift error and does not require contraction. Under the additional contraction condition in Theorem 4.3 , the balanced parameter choices yield 𝒪 ⁡ ( K − 1 ) ⏟ policy iteration + 𝒪 ~ ( n − ζ / ( 2 d + 4 ζ ) ) ⏟ critic + 1 1 − ϱ 𝒪 ~ ( n − ζ / ( d + 1 + 4 ζ ) + n − ζ / ( d + 1 + 4 ζ ) K ) ⏟ actor and inherited error . \underbrace{\mathcal{O}(K^{-1})}_{\text{policy iteration}}+\underbrace{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{-\zeta/(2d+4\zeta)}\right)}_{\text{critic}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\varrho}}\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{-\zeta/(d+1+4\zeta)}+\frac{n^{-\zeta/(d+1+4\zeta)}}{\sqrt{K}}\right)}_{\text{actor and inherited error}}. The actor term combines neural drift regression, finite- m m SNIS estimation, Euler–Maruyama discretization, and the inherited initialization error. The factor ( 1 − ϱ ) − 1 / 2 (1-\varrho)^{-1/2} quantifies the amplification of inherited errors across policy iterations. This simplified rate assumes C snis ​ ( T ) = 𝒪 ~ ​ ( 1 ) C_{\rm snis}(T)=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1) and treats the dimensions, regularity constants, and coverage constants as fixed. This error decomposition is related to both approximate policy-iteration theory ( Xie and Jiang, 2020b ; Zanette et al., 2021 ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) and finite-sample actor–critic theory ( Wu et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gaur et al., 2024 ; Ganesh et al., 2025 ; Chen and Maguluri, 2025 ) . Remark 4.4 . Existing finite-time analyses of actor–critic methods mainly study how critic estimation and function-approximation errors propagate through parameterized policy-gradient dynamics. Two-timescale AC achieves a sample complexity of 𝒪 ~ ( ϵ − 5 / 2 ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-5/2}) for reaching a first-order stationary point under Markovian sampling ( Wu et al., 2020 ) , while single-timescale variants improve this to 𝒪 ~ ​ ( ϵ − 2 ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) and recent extensions also cover deep neural network approximation, compatible critic architectures, and global guarantees in continuous state–action spaces ( Chen and Zhao, 2023 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gaur et al., 2024 ; Ganesh et al., 2025 ) . From a different perspective, Chen and Maguluri (2025) interpret natural policy gradient as approximate policy iteration and establish geometric actor convergence together with an overall 𝒪 ~ ​ ( ϵ − 2 ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) sample complexity up to function-approximation error. SFAC is closer to this policy-iteration viewpoint: each actor step is analyzed relative to an ideal KL-regularized policy-improvement step rather than through first-order stationarity. The additional difficulty is that the improved policy cannot be implemented directly in continuous action spaces; consequently, our analysis controls not only the critic error but also the drift-regression, finite-sample Monte Carlo, and time-discretization errors introduced by the Schrödinger–Föllmer realization. SFAC differs in the source of the actor error. Rather than approximating a policy-gradient direction, it first defines an exact KL-regularized policy-improvement target and then approximates this target with a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer actor. Consequently, Theorem 4.3 propagates critic-estimation error together with errors from drift regression, SNIS, and diffusion discretization, as well as inherited drift error. The resulting guarantee is therefore closer to a finite-sample approximate policy-iteration bound than to a stationary-point guarantee for actor parameters. Direct comparison with the ϵ \epsilon -sample complexities of gradient-based actor–critic methods is not immediate because our analysis separates the budgets K K , n n , m m , and T T . The critic analysis explicitly handles temporal dependence through geometric β \beta -mixing and a blocking argument. The actor-regression analysis instead conditions on the fitted policy and advantage estimator and treats the within-round regression and Monte Carlo samples as conditionally independent.

6 Numerical Experiments
sections.text: This section evaluates the offline-to-online performance and sampling accuracy of SFAC. Section 6.1 describes the tasks, reference methods, model configuration, and evaluation protocol. Section 6.2 compares the offline initialization with online performance on D4RL continuous-control tasks under a fixed interaction protocol. Section 6.3 uses controlled synthetic problems to assess approximation to prescribed advantage-tilted distributions and sensitivity to the diffusion-step count T T and endpoint budget m m .

sections.heading: Tasks and metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate SFAC on six D4RL continuous-control tasks ( Fu et al., 2020 ) : the medium (M) and medium-replay (MR) variants of HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2d. We report D4RL normalized returns. The three environments are illustrated in Figure 1 , and the evaluated dataset variants are listed in Table 2 . (a) Walker2d (b) Hopper (c) HalfCheetah Figure 1: Representative D4RL evaluation environments.

sections.heading: Reference methods.
sections.text: For context, Table 2 includes published results for Cal-QL, a method developed for offline-to-online fine-tuning ( Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Ball et al., 2023 ) , together with the offline final-policy scores of IQL, AWAC, DQL, and IDQL ( Kostrikov et al., 2022 ; Nair et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Because these values were obtained under the interaction budgets and evaluation protocols of their respective studies, they provide contextual reference points rather than a budget-matched ranking. Our controlled comparison is therefore within SFAC: its offline initialization versus its online performance under the protocol specified below.

sections.heading: Model and optimization.
sections.text: The conditional SF actor is an MLP with two hidden layers of width 256 256 and ReLU activations. Actions are generated by simulating the resulting SDE with T = 8 T=8 Euler–Maruyama steps. The critic is an ensemble of 10 10 action-value functions trained with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and minibatches of size 1024 1024 ; the discount factor is γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 . Unless stated otherwise, the drift estimator uses m = 256 m=256 endpoint candidates per diffusion step, and the state-value estimate uses N V = 32 N_{\mathrm{V}}=32 policy samples. We set the KL temperature to λ = 3.0 \lambda=3.0 in all main experiments.

sections.heading: Online evaluation protocol.
sections.text: Each main experiment uses 500 ​ K 500K online environment steps. We evaluate the policy every 10 ​ K 10K steps over 10 10 episodes and run each configuration with three random seeds. To reduce sensitivity to a single noisy checkpoint, the primary online metric is the average of the final five evaluations. For seed r ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } r\in\{1,2,3\} , define J ^ r final \displaystyle\widehat{J}_{r}^{\mathrm{final}} : = 1 5 ​ ∑ j = K − 4 K J ^ r , j , \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{j=K-4}^{K}\widehat{J}_{r,j}, J ^ r , j \displaystyle\widehat{J}_{r,j} : = 1 10 ​ ∑ e = 1 10 R r , j , e , \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{e=1}^{10}R_{r,j,e}, where R r , j , e R_{r,j,e} is the normalized return of evaluation episode e e at checkpoint j j . We report the mean and standard deviation of J ^ r final \widehat{J}_{r}^{\mathrm{final}} across seeds. The maximum online score is reported only as a secondary diagnostic because it is more sensitive to checkpoint selection.

sections.heading: 6.2 Offline-to-Online Performance
sections.text: Table 2 reports the primary within-method comparison. The SFAC final-window score exceeds the score of its offline initialization on all six tasks. The average score increases from 34.09 34.09 to 83.81 83.81 , with the largest absolute gains on Hopper-MR and Walker2d-MR. Because the online score is the average of the last five evaluations for each seed, these improvements are not based on a single selected checkpoint. The published baselines remain contextual: the table does not control for differences in interaction budgets or evaluation protocols across studies. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We formulated KL-regularized policy improvement for diffusion actors using conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer dynamics. A Doob h h -transform converts the exponential advantage tilt into a reference-drift correction, whose posterior-mean form supports sample-based estimation and supervised actor refitting without critic action gradients. The update follows the natural policy-gradient direction locally. Our finite-sample bound separates the effects of critic estimation, drift regression, SNIS, Euler–Maruyama discretization, and inherited actor error on expected average policy suboptimality. Synthetic experiments measure approximation to prescribed tilted targets and sensitivity to sampling budgets. On the evaluated D4RL tasks, online SFAC improves the final-window return of its offline initialization under the reported protocol. Future work may broaden the theoretical guarantees for diffusion-based policy improvement. Extending the framework to more complex control tasks and real-world decision problems would help assess its practical scope and the trade-offs between policy expressiveness and statistical accuracy.

sections.heading: Appendix
sections.text: The appendix provides the derivations and proofs supporting the main text. Appendix A illustrates the interpretation of SFAC in terms of a diffusion-based natural policy-gradient direction. Appendix B derives the conditional SF drift and its estimator. Appendices C and D analyze advantage estimation and actor approximation, respectively. Appendix E combines these bounds in the policy-performance analysis under its stated conditions. Appendix F collects the auxiliary results, and Appendix G gives the offline pretraining algorithm.

sections.text: The algorithm estimates the reference SF drift by regressing the scaled Brownian-bridge terminal displacement on the bridge inputs. Algorithm 3 Offline Pretraining of the SF Drift 1: Input: offline dataset 𝒟 off = { ( s i , a i ) } i = 1 n \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}}=\{(s_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} , drift network b ϕ b_{\phi} , Euler-step count T T , minibatch size B B 2: for each training step do 3: Sample a minibatch ℐ ⊂ { 1 , … , n } \mathcal{I}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\} , | ℐ | = B |\mathcal{I}|=B . 4: for i ∈ ℐ i\in\mathcal{I} do 5: Sample J i ∼ Unif ⁡ { 0 , … , T − 1 } J_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0,\ldots,T-1\} and ε i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d 𝒜 ) \varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{\mathcal{A}}}) , and set t i = J i / T t_{i}=J_{i}/T . 6: Construct y i = t i ​ a i + t i ​ ( 1 − t i ) ​ ε i , u i = a i − y i 1 − t i . y_{i}=t_{i}a_{i}+\sqrt{t_{i}(1-t_{i})}\,\varepsilon_{i},\qquad u_{i}=\frac{a_{i}-y_{i}}{1-t_{i}}. 7: end for 8: Update ϕ \phi using 1 B ​ ∑ i ∈ ℐ ‖ b ϕ ​ ( s i , y i , t i ) − u i ‖ 2 2 . \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\left\|b_{\phi}(s_{i},y_{i},t_{i})-u_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}. 9: end for 10: Output: pretrained drift b ϕ k ← b ϕ b_{\phi_{k}}\leftarrow b_{\phi} .

Email: jinchengying@whu.edu.cn Abstract Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but an advantage-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback–Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the advantage function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob h h -transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. We derive a posterior-mean representation of the correction and estimate it using paired self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). Supervised regression on these drift targets updates the neural actor without critic action gradients. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the effects of critic estimation, neural drift regression, finite-sample SNIS, diffusion discretization, and inherited actor error on expected average policy suboptimality. Synthetic experiments assess the accuracy of approximation to prescribed advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to sampling budgets. On six offline-to-online continuous-control tasks, a reference-anchored implementation achieves higher final-window returns than those of its corresponding offline initialization. Keywords: Offline-to-online RL; diffusion policies; Schrödinger–Föllmer sampling; Doob h h -transform; finite-sample analysis. 1 Introduction Offline RL learns a policy from previously collected transitions without further interaction with the environment. The accuracy of its value estimates depends on the state–action coverage of these data ( Levine et al., 2020 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ; Kostrikov et al., 2022 ) . Offline-to-online (O2O) RL combines offline data or pretrained policies with subsequent online learning ( Nair et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Ball et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . This transition requires adapting to new experience while retaining useful information from the offline data. In the early online stages, value estimates remain influenced by offline coverage: favoring poorly covered actions can amplify estimation error, whereas restrictive policy updates can limit adaptation. Policy representation introduces a further challenge: offline datasets may combine several behavior policies and contain multiple plausible actions at the same state. Diffusion actors accommodate the resulting multimodal conditional action distributions ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . They define policies through a generative process without requiring an explicit conditional density. Policy improvement therefore requires modifying this process to sample from the action distribution prescribed by estimated value information. To formulate this problem, we follow advantage-weighted and product-policy approaches to policy improvement ( Peng et al., 2019 ; Nair et al., 2020 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) and use A π ​ ( s , a ) A^{\pi}(s,a) to measure the quality of an action relative to the current policy. Realizing this KL-regularized update therefore requires a corresponding change in the diffusion drift. Existing generative-policy methods incorporate value information through critic action gradients, actor-parameter optimization, or reweighting of sampled candidate actions ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2023a ; Park et al., 2025 ) . A complementary approach is to estimate the drift implied by the prescribed tilt from policy samples and pointwise advantage evaluations. Such a construction would permit supervised actor fitting without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. Its statistical accuracy, however, depends on both the estimated advantage and the approximation of the target diffusion. Errors from critic estimation, drift learning, and numerical sampling can propagate through successive policy updates. An exact tilting identity alone does not control these effects. This motivates a joint construction and analysis that connects the prescribed target, the learned diffusion drift, and the resulting policy performance. To address these issues, we propose Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online method for KL-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. SFAC represents the current policy as the terminal law of a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer diffusion ( Föllmer, 1985 ; Föllmer, 1986 ; Föllmer, 1988 ) . Reweighting this terminal law induces a change of measure on path space, which a Doob h h -transform realizes through a drift correction ( Doob, 1984 ; Baudoin, 2002 ) . Here h h is the positive conditional expectation, under the reference diffusion, of the terminal reweighting factor given the current diffusion state. Applying this construction to the advantage tilt gives a target diffusion whose terminal law is the prescribed policy update. The learned actor and its numerical sampler approximate this exact representation. Specifically, at iteration k k , let π k \pi_{k} denote the current practical policy and A ^ k \widehat{A}_{k} the minimax Bellman critic’s estimate of its advantage A π k A^{\pi_{k}} . The resulting plug-in target π ¯ k + 1  ar{\pi}_{k+1} satisfies π ¯ k + 1 ​ ( a ∣ s ) ∝ π k ​ ( a ∣ s ) ​ exp ⁡ { A ^ k ​ ( s , a ) / λ }  ar{\pi}_{k+1}(a\mid s)\propto\pi_{k}(a\mid s)\exp\{\widehat{A}_{k}(s,a)/\lambda\} . Here ∝ \propto denotes equality up to a state-dependent normalizing factor. The drift correction is a time-scaled difference between the posterior means under the advantage-tilted and reference distributions. Paired self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) estimates these means from shared terminal-action samples. Adding the resulting Monte Carlo correction to the current learned drift produces regression targets for the updated neural actor. Euler–Maruyama simulation of this actor defines the practical policy π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} , which approximates π ¯ k + 1  ar{\pi}_{k+1} . The actor update therefore uses supervised drift regression without critic action gradients. In the small-update regime, the ideal exponential tilt follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same first-order change in the space of diffusion drifts. We then analyze how the approximation errors affect policy performance. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds for advantage estimation under dependent transition data, actor regression, SNIS, and time discretization. Combining these bounds with the inherited actor error yields a bound on expected average policy suboptimality across iterations. The analysis separates the contributions of the statistical and computational budgets; it does not cover neural-network optimization or replay-buffer management. We complement this analysis with experiments on the sampling construction and its use in online policy refinement. Controlled examples use two- and four-component Gaussian mixtures to assess approximation to specified advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to the endpoint sample size m m and diffusion-step count T T . We also evaluate a reference-anchored implementation on six continuous-control tasks from Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning (D4RL) ( Fu et al., 2020 ) . Under the reported protocol for interaction, replay, and evaluation, its final-window normalized return exceeds that of the corresponding offline initialization on all six tasks. 1.1 Contributions Our contributions are as follows. • A conditional-diffusion formulation of policy improvement. We formulate KL-regularized policy improvement for diffusion actors through a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer process. The exponential advantage tilt defines a terminal change of measure, and the corresponding Doob h h -transform identifies the drift correction that realizes the improved policy. In the small-update regime, the ideal KL step follows the natural policy-gradient direction, while the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. • Sample-based actor learning without critic action gradients. The Doob correction is the difference between advantage-tilted and reference posterior means. We estimate this difference by paired self-normalized importance sampling using current-policy samples and pointwise advantage evaluations, then fit the next drift network by supervised regression. This update does not require critic action gradients. • Finite-sample guarantees. We bound actor estimation error in Wasserstein distance and reverse KL divergence, separating the contributions of neural drift regression, finite-sample SNIS, Euler–Maruyama discretization, and inherited reference-drift error. Combining this result with critic estimation under dependent transition data yields a bound on expected average policy suboptimality across policy iterations. • Empirical evidence. We evaluate our method for offline-to-online policy improvement. Synthetic experiments evaluate approximation to prescribed advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to the endpoint-sample and diffusion-step budgets. On six D4RL continuous-control tasks, the reference-anchored implementation improves its final-window performance relative to the corresponding offline initialization. 1.2 Related Work Offline and offline-to-online RL. Offline RL addresses distribution shift through conservative action-value estimation, behavior-regularized policy learning, or implicit policy extraction ( Kumar et al., 2020 ; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Kostrikov et al., 2022 ) . The transition to online learning also requires preserving useful offline behavior while adapting to new experience. Advantage-weighted actor–critic (AWAC) uses weighted maximum-likelihood actor updates, calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL) controls the scale of conservative action-value estimates, and policy expansion (PEX) combines a frozen offline policy with a learnable policy ( Nair et al., 2020 ; Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . RL with prior data (RLPD) instead incorporates offline transitions directly into online off-policy training, without requiring offline pretraining ( Ball et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion models can also augment the training distribution: synthetic experience replay (SynthER) generates additional replay data, whereas energy-guided diffusion sampling (EDIS) guides synthetic transitions toward the current online distribution ( Lu et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . These methods generate transitions; SFAC instead updates conditional action distributions. Fitted policy iteration and minimax Bellman methods relate estimation error to policy performance under approximation and coverage conditions ( Antos et al., 2008 ; Xie and Jiang, 2020b ) . Deep approximate policy iteration further combines neural approximation, Bellman-residual estimation under dependent data, and error propagation ( Jiao et al., 2025 ) . Minimax off-policy evaluation separately studies the statistical estimation of policy returns ( Uehara et al., 2020 ; Uehara et al., 2021 ) , while policy-finetuning theory quantifies the role of reference-policy coverage in sample-efficient online adaptation ( Xie et al., 2021b ) . SFAC addresses the additional actor-learning and numerical-sampling errors introduced by conditional diffusion policy updates. Generative policies. Denoising and score-based diffusion models provide flexible distributional representations ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Diffuser and Decision Diffuser generate trajectories for planning, whereas Diffusion Policy generates observation-conditioned action sequences ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) . For action-level policy improvement, Diffusion-QL combines denoising regression with action-value maximization ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Implicit diffusion Q-learning (IDQL) reweights candidates from a diffusion behavior model and also considers online fine-tuning ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Contrastive energy prediction (CEP) learns intermediate energy guidance for Q-guided policy optimization (QGPO), with population consistency under unlimited model capacity and data ( Lu et al., 2023a ) . Diffusion actor–critic (DAC) expresses behavior-constrained policy improvement as noise regression with a critic-action-gradient correction ( Fang et al., 2025 ) . Classifier-free guidance for RL (CFGRL) instead trains an optimality-conditioned generative model and adjusts its guidance strength at sampling time ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Flow Q-Learning trains a one-step actor using a flow behavior model and includes O2O evaluation ( Park et al., 2025 ) ; diffusion policy policy optimization (DPPO) fine-tunes diffusion policies by applying policy optimization to coupled denoising and environment dynamics ( Ren et al., 2025 ) . These methods differ in how action-value information enters the policy update. SFAC uses paired SNIS to estimate posterior-mean drift corrections and refits a conditional Schrödinger–Föllmer actor by supervised regression. Its distinguishing feature is this drift-target construction, rather than KL regularization or actor refitting alone. Regularized updates and controlled diffusion. Relative-entropy policy search and KL-constrained policy optimization motivate exponential reweighting relative to a reference distribution ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2019 ) . Maximum-entropy RL promotes policy entropy, while regularized Bellman theory provides a broader framework for penalty-based updates and their error propagation ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ; Geist et al., 2019 ) . On path space, Föllmer’s entropy construction and the Doob h h -transform connect terminal reweighting to a change in diffusion drift ( Föllmer, 1985 ; Föllmer, 1986 ; Föllmer, 1988 ; Doob, 1984 ) . Schrödinger–Föllmer samplers realize a target law at a finite terminal time, without an ergodic limit; their nonasymptotic analyses allow non-log-concave targets under suitable regularity conditions ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Jiao et al., 2026 ) . Diffusion Schrödinger bridges address the related problem of entropy-regularized transport between endpoint distributions ( De Bortoli et al., 2021 ) . For pretrained diffusion models, entropy-regularized control yields reward-based fine-tuning objectives ( Uehara et al., 2024a ) , and feedback-efficient methods combine reward learning, exploration, and generative updates with regret guarantees ( Uehara et al., 2024b ) . Recent theory establishes regularity preservation and convergence of control-policy iteration ( Han et al., 2025 ) , regression-based statistical guarantees for diffusion fine-tuning ( Mou, 2025 ) , and nonasymptotic guidance and distributional bounds for learned Doob h h -transforms ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . Finite-particle approximations can nevertheless bias the intended tilt, even in tractable Gaussian examples ( Dandapanthula and Boffi, 2026 ) . An exact change-of-measure identity therefore does not establish the accuracy of an estimated and discretized actor. SFAC complements these results by propagating Bellman-critic, posterior-mean, drift-regression, and discretization errors through successive policy updates. The resulting guarantee concerns expected average suboptimality under regularity, coverage, and stability conditions, not improvement of every fitted policy.
